title: The history of the vacuum flask
tagline: From a tube of mercury in 1643 to a laboratory bottle of liquid air in 1892, and the steel flask in every Indian office bag.
intro: To keep something hot or cold you must stop heat leaving by touch, by moving air and by glowing. Scientists learned to make a vacuum in the 1600s and found in 1804 that shiny surfaces glow very little. In 1892 James Dewar put both ideas into one double-walled glass flask to keep liquefied gases cold. German glassblowers turned it into an everyday bottle called Thermos, the name became an ordinary word, and stainless steel made the flask tough enough for school bags and trains.

eras.name: Emptiness and glowing heat
eras.summary: Scientists make the first vacuums, prove that air presses hard on everything, and discover that heat radiates, more from dull surfaces than shiny ones.

eras.name: The scientist's flask
eras.summary: Chemists racing to liquefy gases need bottles that keep them cold. Double walls with a vacuum between them, silvered like mirrors, do the job.

eras.name: Thermos for everyone
eras.summary: German glassblowers put the lab flask in a metal case and give it a name. Licensed companies make it in Europe and North America.

eras.name: A brand becomes a word
eras.summary: So many people call every vacuum bottle a thermos that a US court rules the lower-case word belongs to everyone.

eras.name: Steel flasks and new cousins
eras.summary: Vacuum insulation goes into rockets and windows, stainless steel replaces fragile glass, and India writes its own standard for the steel flask.

events.title: A tube with nothing at the top
events.text: Torricelli filled a glass tube with mercury and turned it upside down in a dish. The mercury fell a little and left an empty space at the top: one of the first lasting vacuums made by people. The weight of the air outside held the rest of the column up.
events.why: It showed that a vacuum could exist, and that the air around us presses hard on everything.

events.title: The first air pump
events.text: Guericke, the mayor of Magdeburg, built a piston pump with one-way valves that could suck the air out of a sealed vessel. His first wooden and metal containers leaked or were crushed by the air outside, so he moved to strong copper spheres.
events.why: Every vacuum flask is pumped out by a descendant of this machine.

events.title: Horses can't pull the hemispheres apart
events.text: Guericke fitted two copper half-spheres together and pumped out the air. Accounts say teams of horses pulling on each side could not separate them until he let the air back in. The number of horses and the size of the spheres differ between accounts.
events.why: It made the push of the atmosphere, more than 100,000 pascals, something everyone could see.

events.title: Shiny surfaces glow less
events.text: Leslie filled a metal cube with boiling water and gave its sides different surfaces. The blackened side gave off the most radiant heat and the polished metal side very little, which he measured with his own differential thermometer. He won the Royal Society's Rumford Medal in 1805.
events.why: It is why the walls of every flask that face the vacuum are silvered or polished.

events.title: A vacuum goblet
events.text: Twenty years before his famous flask, Dewar worked with the physicist Peter Tait on a vacuum-insulated goblet to keep substances warm, according to the Royal Institution.
events.why: Dewar came back to the same idea when he needed to keep things cold.

events.title: Glow grows with the fourth power
events.text: Stefan noticed in other scientists' measurements that the heat radiated by a hot body rises with the fourth power of its absolute temperature. Double the kelvin and it radiates sixteen times as much.
events.why: It lets us calculate how many watts a flask's walls radiate across the vacuum.

events.title: A vacuum-jacketed vessel in a textbook
events.text: German sources credit the chemistry teacher Weinhold with describing an evacuated double-walled vessel for liquefied gases in his 1881 book of physics demonstrations. Accounts disagree on how it relates to Dewar's flask; Dewar is usually thought to have invented his own independently.
events.why: Good ideas often turn up more than once when many people face the same problem.

events.title: Boltzmann explains the fourth power
events.text: Stefan's former student Boltzmann derived the fourth-power law from thermodynamics and the electromagnetic theory of light. It has been called the Stefan–Boltzmann law ever since.
events.why: A law with a reason behind it can be trusted beyond the range it was measured in.

events.title: Dewar's vacuum flask
events.text: Dewar sealed one glass flask inside another with a vacuum between them, to keep liquefied gases cold long enough to study them. It was shown at the Royal Institution for the first time on Christmas Day 1892. He later narrowed the neck and silvered the walls. He never patented it.
events.why: It is the ancestor of every flask, and laboratories still call them Dewars.

events.title: Liquid hydrogen, kept in a flask
events.text: With his own machinery and his vacuum flasks, Dewar collected liquid hydrogen for the first time, at about −253 °C. He made solid hydrogen the following year.
events.why: Without a bottle that slowed heat this well, the coldest liquids could not have been kept at all.

events.title: A flask for everyday use
events.text: Burger, a glassblower, received a German patent for a vacuum flask for daily use, protected by a metal case. Dewar later went to court over the invention and lost: he had never patented it.
events.why: It moved the vacuum flask out of the laboratory and into kitchens and lunch boxes.

events.title: The name Thermos
events.text: Burger registered the trademark Thermos, from the Greek thermē, heat. The company's own account says the name was chosen in a public competition and sent in by a resident of Munich.
events.why: A catchy name helped the flask spread, so well that the name became a word.

events.title: Thermos GmbH
events.who: Reinhold Burger, Albert Aschenbrenner and Gustav Robert Paalen
events.text: Burger founded the company Thermos GmbH with Albert Aschenbrenner and Gustav Robert Paalen, who improved and patented domestic designs. Companies in the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom bought licences for their own markets.
events.why: Licensed makers on two continents turned a German invention into an international product.

events.title: A flask factory in Connecticut
events.text: The American company signed the contract for a large factory in Norwich, where vacuum bottles were mass-produced for decades. The Norwich plants closed in 1988.
events.why: Mass production made flasks cheap enough for workers' lunch boxes.

events.title: A first fight over the word
events.text: The company won a narrow court case against the retailer W. T. Grant over the word, and registered the trademark in 1923. Yet from about 1910 to 1922 its own advertising had used "thermos" as an everyday word.
events.why: Using your own brand name as a common noun can cost you the brand.

events.title: A judge rules "thermos" is generic
events.text: In 1958 Aladdin Industries announced it would sell "thermos bottles" and was sued. In 1962 Judge Anderson ruled that the lower-case word thermos had become the ordinary name for a vacuum bottle in the United States.
events.why: It is one of the best-known cases of a trademark turning into a common word.

events.title: The appeal court agrees
events.who: US Court of Appeals, Second Circuit
events.text: The appeal court upheld the ruling. A survey had found that about 75% of American adults called such a bottle a thermos and only about 12% knew it was a trademark. Aladdin could use "thermos" only in lower case, never with "original" or "genuine", and the company kept its capital-T Thermos.
events.why: A word that everyone uses can no longer belong to one company, at least in that country.

events.title: Vacuum-jacketed rocket tanks
events.text: Propellant tanks of the Saturn rockets in the 1960s and 1970s used the vacuum-flask idea to keep their super-cold fuels from boiling away.
events.why: The physics that keeps chai hot also kept rocket fuel cold on the way to the Moon.

events.title: Sealing a steel flask in a furnace
events.text: Nippon Sanso patented a way to make metal vacuum bottles in one step: the two steel shells are brazed together in a vacuum furnace at about 1,050 °C, and a getter powder such as titanium hydride then soaks up the leftover gas, mostly hydrogen. The patent was filed in 1978 and granted in 1979.
events.why: Cheap, reliable sealing made the all-steel flask possible.

events.title: The first stainless steel vacuum bottle
events.text: The Japanese industrial-gas company developed the first stainless steel vacuum-insulated bottle. Steel flasks shrug off knocks that would shatter a glass refill.
events.why: It is the ancestor of the steel flask carried to offices, schools and trains across India today.

events.title: The Thermos companies change hands
events.text: Nippon Sanso bought the Thermos companies in Japan, the UK, Canada and Australia, and later the original Thermos GmbH in Germany, which had been behind the Iron Curtain from 1945 until German reunification.
events.why: The maker of the first steel flask came to own the oldest flask brand.

events.title: Vacuum glazing
events.who: University of Sydney; Nippon Sheet Glass
events.text: Researchers at the University of Sydney reported the first vacuum glazing in 1989: two panes a fraction of a millimetre apart, held by tiny pillars, with a vacuum between. Nippon Sheet Glass licensed it and put it on sale in 1996.
events.why: A window built like a flask lets far less heat through than ordinary double glazing.

events.title: India's standard for the steel flask
events.text: BIS published IS 17526:2021 for domestic stainless steel vacuum flasks and bottles. It covers the materials of the inner bottle, case and stopper, and tests for keeping heat and cold, leaking, corrosion and knocks.
events.why: It sets the bar for the flasks millions of Indians carry every day.

people.name: Evangelista Torricelli
people.note: Made a lasting vacuum at the top of a column of mercury.

people.name: Otto von Guericke
people.note: Built the first air pump and showed the force of the atmosphere with his hemispheres.

people.name: John Leslie
people.note: Showed that a polished surface radiates far less heat than a blackened one.

people.name: Josef Stefan
people.note: Found that radiated heat grows with the fourth power of temperature.

people.name: Ludwig Boltzmann
people.note: Explained Stefan's fourth-power law from thermodynamics and the theory of light.

people.name: James Dewar
people.note: Invented the vacuum flask in 1892 to keep liquefied gases cold, and first liquefied hydrogen.

people.name: Adolf Ferdinand Weinhold
people.note: Described a vacuum-jacketed vessel in 1881, by German accounts.

people.name: Reinhold Burger
people.note: Patented the everyday vacuum flask in 1903 and registered the name Thermos.

facts: Dewar's original 1892 flask is on display in the Faraday Museum at the Royal Institution in London.
Dewar was nominated for a Nobel Prize several times but never won one, and he never patented his flask.
In the 1963 court case, about three in four American adults called a vacuum bottle a thermos, and only about one in eight knew it was a trademark.
Thermos is still a registered trademark in more than a hundred countries, even though the lower-case word is generic in the United States.
Pumping out half the air in a flask's gap does nothing: the gas only stops conducting once it is a hundred thousand times thinner than air.
